page.title: Lesson Overview
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 7 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Integrated Publication-Ready Portfolio Preparation

Lesson Focus

Lesson 7: Integrated Publication-Ready Portfolio Preparation

Primary Standards: MLA.CW.PUB.01 — Online collaborative publication; MLA.CW.REV.01 — Revision from feedback.

Supporting Standards: MLA.CW.PUB.02 — Format-specific quality work; MLA.CW.REV.02 — Clarity, cohesion, and conventions; MLA.CW.COM.01 — Author presentation of creative work.

What You Will Learn

  • Select work using evidence rather than attachment alone.
  • Translate feedback into purposeful revision.
  • Audit craft, conventions, accessibility, and presentation together.
  • Write a portfolio note that explains growth with specific evidence.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 7 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
portfolioA purposeful collection selected to demonstrate quality, range, and growth.The portfolio includes polished work and evidence of development.
curationThe deliberate selection, ordering, and framing of items for an audience.The writer opens with a strong piece and groups related work.
artifactA specific piece of work or evidence included in a portfolio.A marked draft is an artifact showing revision.
revision trailEvidence showing how a work changed from draft to final form and why.Drafts and notes create a revision trail.
editorial priorityA ranked need that guides which revisions should happen first.Repairing an unclear ending takes priority over punctuation.
cohesionThe clear connection among ideas, sections, or portfolio items.A recurring theme gives the collection cohesion.
accessibilityDesign that allows people with differing needs to perceive and use the work.Readable contrast and alt text improve accessibility.
metadataDescriptive information such as title, author, genre, date, or file label.Each file’s metadata identifies its genre and revision date.
proofreadTo inspect a near-final work for errors in language, formatting, and consistency.The writer proofreads after completing major revisions.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which choice shows purposeful curation?

A. Include every draft in the order it was created.

This collects material but does not select, order, or frame it for an audience.

B. Select artifacts that show range and growth, then order them to create a clear reading path.

Correct. The writer makes deliberate choices about selection, sequence, and audience experience.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 7 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: From Draft Collection to Coherent Portfolio

Step 1 — Curate with Criteria

  1. List candidate works and the standards each demonstrates.
  2. Score each for craft quality, revision growth, range, and readiness.
  3. Select the strongest set—not merely the newest or longest pieces.
  4. Identify any gap, such as no evidence of dialogue, structure, or feedback-based revision.

Selection Matrix

CriterionEvidence to seek
QualityControlled language, structure, voice, and conventions
GrowthA meaningful draft-to-final change with rationale
RangeDifferent genres, techniques, purposes, or audiences
ReadinessNo unresolved high-impact weakness

Pause and Choose: Curate with Evidence

A writer must choose between a polished recent poem and an older story that shows a major, well-documented revision. Which portfolio decision is strongest?

A. Include only the newest work because recency automatically proves quality and growth.
Weaker choice. Recency is not a portfolio criterion. It may hide stronger evidence of craft range or meaningful development.
B. Evaluate both against quality, growth, range, and readiness, then include the story if its revision trail fills an important evidence gap.
Stronger choice. The decision is criterion-based and purposeful. A coherent portfolio selects artifacts for what they demonstrate, not merely when they were written.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 2 — Revise by Impact

Sort feedback into four levels: meaning and purpose → structure and development → sentence craft → correctness and format. Revise in that order. Polishing punctuation before repairing a missing turning point wastes effort.

Step 3 — Build a Revision Trail

For every major change, save three pieces of evidence: Before, After, and Why. The “why” must name the reader problem and the intended improvement.

Pause and Choose: Explain Revision Growth

Which revision-trail note demonstrates meaningful growth?

A. “Before, the conflict arrived on page four. After reader confusion, I moved the failed promise into the opening scene so later choices have a visible cause.”
Stronger choice. It shows before and after, identifies a reader problem, and explains how the structural change improves cause and effect.
B. “I changed many things and made the story much better.”
Weaker choice. The claim is too general to verify. It names neither an artifact nor specific evidence, reasoning, or effect.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 4 — Publication Audit

  • Content: complete, accurate, ethically represented.
  • Craft: purposeful language, pacing, form, and voice.
  • Conventions: grammar and mechanics support meaning.
  • Design: readable font, spacing, headings, captions, and consistent order.
  • Accessibility: descriptive links, text alternatives for meaningful images, sufficient contrast, and no meaning conveyed by color alone.
  • Files: clear metadata, stable file type, working links, and logical names.

Step 5 — Write the Portfolio Note

Use the pattern Claim → Artifact → Specific evidence → Growth insight → Next goal. Avoid vague statements such as “I became a better writer.” Show exactly what improved.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 7 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Portfolio Decisions

Example 1 — Choosing the Stronger Artifact

Candidate A: a polished 1,800-word story with vivid description but little evidence of revision.

Candidate B: a 1,200-word story whose revision trail shows a confusing flashback reorganized into a controlled nonlinear structure.

  1. Identify the portfolio purpose: demonstrate quality and revision growth.
  2. Compare evidence: A is polished; B demonstrates craft, feedback use, and growth.
  3. Decision: include B if its final quality is strong enough.
  4. Portfolio note: cite the exact reordering and its effect on reader orientation.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which artifact best demonstrates both quality and revision growth?

A. The longer, polished story, because length and vivid description prove stronger writing.
Weaker response. This relies on surface polish and length without evidence of the writer’s revision decisions or growth.
B. The shorter story, if its final quality is strong, because its revision trail shows a confusing flashback transformed into controlled nonlinear structure.
Stronger response. This choice uses the portfolio purpose as a criterion and identifies concrete before-and-after evidence while maintaining a quality threshold.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Prioritizing Feedback

Feedback: (a) “The climax arrives before the central conflict is clear.” (b) “Change two commas.” (c) “The blue wallpaper detail is memorable.”

  1. Classify: (a) structure, (b) correctness, (c) strength to preserve.
  2. Prioritize the structural problem first.
  3. Revise by planting the conflict earlier and testing whether the climax now feels earned.
  4. Then correct punctuation without removing the effective wallpaper image.

Reasoning: Revision is not accepting every comment equally; it is diagnosing impact.

Example 3 — Publication and Accessibility Audit

Draft portfolio page: “FinalStoryNEW2.docx,” decorative script font, a photograph with no caption or text alternative, and a link labeled “click here.”

  1. Rename the file RiverGlass_Final_AnikaChen.pdf.
  2. Use a readable heading and body font with consistent contrast.
  3. Add concise alternative text describing the meaningful content of the photograph.
  4. Replace “click here” with a descriptive label such as “Read the revision reflection.”
  5. Open every file and link in a clean browser view before release.

Principle: A work is not publication-ready if the audience cannot reliably access or navigate it.

Transfer Checklist

For each artifact, answer: Why this piece? What changed? What proves the improvement? How will the audience encounter it?

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: Choose between a polished poem with no drafts and a strong scene with documented feedback and revision for a growth portfolio. Defend one choice.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: I would choose the scene if its final craft is strong because the drafts show how feedback led to a purposeful change; the poem may fit a best-work portfolio but offers little growth evidence.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 7 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Integrated Publication-Ready Portfolio Preparation

Purpose

Curate, revise, organize, and frame a coherent portfolio that demonstrates craft, range, and growth.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Use precise evidence from your own work and the source provided.

Source for Your Work

Portfolio challenge: Select work that demonstrates range and growth—not merely the highest-scoring pieces—and guide a reader through the collection with clear organization and reflection.

1. Plan Before You Work

DecisionYour Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each clearly.
Most important craft or communication needName the need and evidence.
Success indicatorDescribe what an effective result will do for a reader.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Include every draft in chronological order and let the reader decide what matters.
B. Select purposeful evidence, polish each piece, organize the collection for a reader, and explain growth using specific before-and-after evidence.

3. Apply the Lesson

Design a publication-ready mini-portfolio with three creative pieces or substantial excerpts. Include a contents plan, rationale for selection and order, revision priorities for each piece, and a 250–350 word reflective introduction citing specific craft growth.

4. Revise with Purpose

Audit the portfolio for coherence and reader experience. Revise one selection, sequence, or framing choice and justify the change.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to a specific creative product.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on readers.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves the work, not only its appearance.
TOR Help

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Integrated Publication-Ready Portfolio Preparation

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: The Uneven Portfolio

A writer’s portfolio contains a polished poem, an unrevised first-draft story, a strong script with inconsistent formatting, and an author statement that lists assignments without explaining growth. The pieces are individually promising, but the collection does not yet communicate a coherent identity or meet publication standards.

A portfolio is a deliberately selected and organized body of work. Publication-ready means content, conventions, formatting, attribution, accessibility, and presentation have been purposefully completed for an audience.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Identify the three highest-priority revisions and justify the order in which the writer should complete them.
  2. What unifying idea could the author statement develop without pretending that every piece is the same?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which approach creates a more purposeful publication-ready portfolio?

A. Include every draft in chronological order because a larger portfolio always appears more accomplished.
B. Select strong evidence of range and growth, revise each piece to a common quality threshold, and organize the collection around a clear rationale.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Prepare an integrated mini-portfolio containing three original works in at least two formats.

  1. Selection: Choose pieces that demonstrate range, growth, and intentional craft.
  2. Revision: Complete a substantive revision and final conventions pass on each piece.
  3. Organization: Create a title page, table of contents, purposeful sequence, and consistent visual system.
  4. Context notes: Write 100–150 words per piece explaining purpose, audience, craft, feedback used, and key revision.
  5. Quality control: Verify format conventions, attribution, accessibility, and working navigation.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Conduct a portfolio-level consistency pass. Correct one inconsistency in design or labeling and one weakness in the sequence; explain the reader effect.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
